claim: The OSCA/TMEM63 family has been identified as mechanically activated ion channels.
source: The dimeric two-pore OSCA/TMEM63 family has recently been identified as mechanically activated ion channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established finding.

claim: OSCA/TMEM63 channels are dimeric.
source: The dimeric two-pore OSCA/TMEM63 family has recently been identified as mechanically activated ion channels.
evidence: The dimeric nature is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: OSCA/TMEM63 channels have two pores.
source: The dimeric two-pore OSCA/TMEM63 family has recently been identified as mechanically activated ion channels.
evidence: The two-pore architecture is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: Several structural elements of OSCA1.2 are potentially involved in sensing membrane tension.
source: Previously, based on the unique features of the structure of OSCA1.2, we postulated the potential involvement of several structural elements in sensing membrane tension (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract with citation to previous work.

claim: OSCA1, 2, and 3 clades are activated by membrane stretch in cell-attached patches.
source: Interestingly, while OSCA1, 2, and 3 clades are activated by membrane stretch in cell-attached patches (i.e. they are stretch-activated channels), they differ in their ability to transduce membrane deformation induced by a blunt probe (poking).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: OSCA1, 2, and 3 clades differ in their ability to transduce membrane deformation induced by poking.
source: Interestingly, while OSCA1, 2, and 3 clades are activated by membrane stretch in cell-attached patches (i.e. they are stretch-activated channels), they differ in their ability to transduce membrane deformation induced by a blunt probe (poking).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The structure of Arabidopsis thaliana OSCA3.1 was solved using cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, in an effort to understand the domains contributing to mechanical signal transduction, we used cryo-electron microscopy to solve the structure of Arabidopsis thaliana (At) OSCA3.1, which, unlike AtOSCA1.2, only produced stretch- but not poke-activated currents in our initial characterization (Murthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a method used in the study.

claim: AtOSCA3.1 only produced stretch-activated currents but not poke-activated currents in initial characterization.
source: Here, in an effort to understand the domains contributing to mechanical signal transduction, we used cryo-electron microscopy to solve the structure of Arabidopsis thaliana (At) OSCA3.1, which, unlike AtOSCA1.2, only produced stretch- but not poke-activated currents in our initial characterization (Murthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract with citation to previous work.

claim: Mutagenesis of conserved and divergent putative mechanosensitive features of OSCA1.2 reveals selective disruption of poke-activated currents without considerable effects on stretch-activated currents.
source: Mutagenesis and electrophysiological assessment of conserved and divergent putative mechanosensitive features of OSCA1.2 reveal a selective disruption of the macroscopic currents elicited by poking without considerable effects on stretch-activated currents (SAC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: The amphipathic helix is involved in the response to poking in OSCA1.2.
source: Our results support the involvement of the amphipathic helix and lipid-interacting residues in the membrane fenestration in the response to poking.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Lipid-interacting residues in the membrane fenestration are involved in the response to poking in OSCA1.2.
source: Our results support the involvement of the amphipathic helix and lipid-interacting residues in the membrane fenestration in the response to poking.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The amphipathic helix and lipid-interacting residues in the membrane fenestration are potential sources of functional diversity within the OSCA family.
source: Our findings position these two structural elements as potential sources of functional diversity within the family.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Mechanically activated ion channels are capable of sensing mechanical stimuli and transducing this information to the cell as electrochemical signals.
source: Mechanically activated (MA) ion channels are capable of sensing mechanical stimuli and transducing this information to the cell as electrochemical signals (Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: MA ion channels are diverse and capable of responding to different stimuli such as osmotic stress, membrane deformation, touch, and hearing.
source: MA ion channels are diverse and capable of responding to different stimuli such as osmotic stress, membrane deformation, touch, and hearing (Haswell et al., 2011; Ranade et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: OSCA/TMEM63 is a conserved family of MA ion channels spanning several eukaryotic clades.
source: In our previous work, we identified OSCA/TMEM63 as a conserved family of MA ion channels spanning several eukaryotic clades and having considerable diversity in the plant kingdom, where species commonly have more than one paralog.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referencing previous work.

claim: OSCA/TMEM63 family has considerable diversity in the plant kingdom.
source: In our previous work, we identified OSCA/TMEM63 as a conserved family of MA ion channels spanning several eukaryotic clades and having considerable diversity in the plant kingdom, where species commonly have more than one paralog.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction referencing previous work.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana has 15 OSCA/TMEM63 members.

source: For example, Arabidopsis thaliana has 15 members (Murthy et al., 2018) and Oryza sativa L. japonica (rice), 11 (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: OSCA channels can respond to membrane stretch more robustly than hypertonicity.
source: We demonstrated these channels can respond to membrane stretch even more robustly than hypertonicity, originally thought to be the relevant stimulus, with some members (OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2) also able to respond to poke (Murthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: OSCA1.1 and OSCA1.2 are able to respond to poke.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The structure of OSCA1.2 was solved in a closed state in both detergent (LMNG) and nanodiscs at high-resolution using cryo-EM.
source: We used cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to solve the structure of OSCA1.2 in a closed state in both detergent (LMNG) and nanodiscs at high-resolution, identifying a new architecture for MA ion channels that is structurally homologous to TMEM16 proteins (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: OSCA1.2 has a new architecture for MA ion channels that is structurally homologous to TMEM16 proteins.
source: We used cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to solve the structure of OSCA1.2 in a closed state in both detergent (LMNG) and nanodiscs at high-resolution, identifying a new architecture for MA ion channels that is structurally homologous to TMEM16 proteins (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: OSCAs are dimeric and each subunit has a pore lined by transmembrane helices 3–7.
source: Similar to the TMEM16 family, OSCAs are dimeric and each subunit has a pore lined by transmembrane helices (TMs) 3–7, instead of a single pore along the symmetry axes (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Maity et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: OSCAs have a pore for each subunit instead of a single pore along the symmetry axes.
source: Similar to the TMEM16 family, OSCAs are dimeric and each subunit has a pore lined by transmembrane helices (TMs) 3–7, instead of a single pore along the symmetry axes (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Maity et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: A hydrophobic gate on the extracellular half of the pore blocks ion flow in OSCAs.
source: A hydrophobic gate on the extracellular half of the pore blocks ion flow.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a structural feature.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations support the placement of the pore and position lipids along an opening of the pore pathway in the transmembrane domain of OSCA1.2.
source: Additionally, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations support our placement of the pore and position lipids along an opening of the pore pathway in the transmembrane domain (TMD; Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The amphipathic helix located in the first intracellular loop might be involved in sensing membrane deformation in OSCA1.2.
source: Based on the unique structural characteristics of OSCA1.2, we proposed that two features might be involved in sensing membrane deformation: the amphipathic helix (AH) located in the first intracellular loop, and the Beam-Like Domain (BLD), composed of the two cytoplasmic membrane-parallel helices and a hydrophobic hook that connects them and re-inserts itself into the membrane (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The Beam-Like Domain (BLD) might be involved in sensing membrane deformation in OSCA1.2.
source: Based on the unique structural characteristics of OSCA1.2, we proposed that two features might be involved in sensing membrane deformation: the amphipathic helix (AH) located in the first intracellular loop, and the Beam-Like Domain (BLD), composed of the two cytoplasmic membrane-parallel helices and a hydrophobic hook that connects them and re-inserts itself into the membrane (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The BLD is composed of two cytoplasmic membrane-parallel helices and a hydrophobic hook that connects them and re-inserts itself into the membrane.
source: Based on the unique structural characteristics of OSCA1.2, we proposed that two features might be involved in sensing membrane deformation: the amphipathic helix (AH) located in the first intracellular loop, and the Beam-Like Domain (BLD), composed of the two cytoplasmic membrane-parallel helices and a hydrophobic hook that connects them and re-inserts itself into the membrane (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The amphipathic helix and BLD could serve as sensors of mechanical stimuli and transmit the signal to the pore through interactions with the TMD.
source: Due to the close association of these two elements to the membrane, we reasoned that they could serve as sensors of mechanical stimuli and transmit the signal to the pore through interactions with the TMD.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a hypothesis.

claim: A fenestration allows the membrane access to the pore in OSCA1.2.
source: Additionally, a fenestration allows the membrane access to the pore, and MD simulations placed lipids in close association with four positively charged residues in this area suggesting a potential role in gating (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: MD simulations placed lipids in close association with four positively charged residues in the fenestration area of OSCA1.2, suggesting a potential role in gating.

claim: OSCA3.1 is the first reported OSCA gene.
source: Here, we used cryo-EM to determine a high-resolution structure of AtOSCA3.1, the first reported OSCA gene (Kiyosue et al., 1994), in nanodiscs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: OSCA3.1 responded to stretch but not poke in initial characterization.

claim: Structure-function analyses revealed the involvement of the AH and the lipid-interacting residues in the pore pathway of OSCA1.2 in the ability of the channel to respond to membrane deformation by poking.
source: Structure-function analyses revealed the involvement of the AH and the lipid-interacting residues in the pore pathway of OSCA1.2 in the ability of the channel to respond to membrane deformation by poking.

claim: The AH and lipid-interacting residues in the pore pathway may serve to tune the response of OSCA/TMEM63 members to diverse stimuli.
source: Our results suggest that these features are not only important for activation of OSCA1.2 by poking but may serve to tune the response of OSCA/TMEM63 members to diverse stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A model of 537 out of 724 residues of OSCA3.1 was built from the cryo-EM reconstruction.

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Modification of OSCA1.2 residues to match those of OSCA3.1 (OSCA1.2K435I/K536I) produced an OSCA3.1-like phenotype.
source: Modification of OSCA1.2 residues to match those of OSCA3.1 (OSCA1.2K435I/K536I) produced an OSCA3.1-like phenotype (MA currents are observed in response to stretch but rarely to poke).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: OSCA1.2K435I/K536I mutant channels are not completely insensitive to poking but appear to have a very high threshold to activate.
source: These mutant channels are not completely insensitive to poking but appear to have a very high threshold to activate, one that is often beyond the point of cell rupture by the stimulus (similar to that seen with OSCA1.2W75K/L80E).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: TM4 in TMEM16 lipid scramblases and TM6 in both TMEM16 scramblases and channels undergo conformational changes during activation.
source: Notably, TM4 in TMEM16 lipid scramblases and TM6 in both TMEM16 scramblases and channels undergo conformational changes during activation (Alvadia et al., 2019; Kalienkova et al., 2019; Paulino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The loss of positive charges in OSCA3.1 may weaken the interactions between residues and lipids.
source: The loss of positive charges in OSCA3.1 may weaken the interactions between residues and lipids, similar to MscS where charge neutralization of the lipid facing residue R59 by the introduction of a leucine strongly altered gating, potentially by disturbing a salt bridge with a lipid phosphate (Flegler et al., 2021; Rasmussen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: A weaker interaction between residues and lipids could decrease the tension generated by the lipids upon mechanical stimulus, hence increasing the force needed to open the channel.
source: A weaker interaction could decrease the tension generated by the lipids upon mechanical stimulus, hence increasing the force needed to open the channel, as seen in our poke experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: By disturbing the coupling of the AH with the lipid bilayer, a greater stimulus might be needed to activate the channel.
source: A similar argument could be made for the AH of OSCAs: by disturbing its coupling with the lipid bilayer, a greater stimulus might be needed to activate the channel.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: The membrane of a plant cell contains a different lipid composition than that of HEK293 cells.
source: It is also important to note that the membrane of a plant cell contains a different lipid composition than that of HEK293 cells used in our assays, and thus these lipids, or association with the plant cell wall, may alter how these channels respond to physiological stimuli in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a caveat.

claim: The phenotypes of OSCA1.2W75K/L80E and OSCA1.2K435I/K536I suggest a mechanism recruited by poking is no longer able to adequately activate these mutant channels.
source: The phenotypes of OSCA1.2W75K/L80E and OSCA1.2K435I/K536I suggest a mechanism recruited by poking is no longer able to adequately activate OSCA1.2W75K/L80E and OSCA1.2K435I/K536I channels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Poking and stretch stimuli are sensed by different features of OSCA channels.
source: Our results suggest that these stimuli are sensed by different features of OSCA channels, akin to the well-studied ThermoTRP channels (Bandell et al., 2006; Fernández-Ballester et al., 2023; Jordt and Julius, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: Polymodal activation mechanisms have been recently reported for the MA channel PIEZO2 where a mutagenesis approach revealed differential effects on the ability to respond to poking and stretch.
source: Polymodal activation mechanisms have been recently reported for the MA channel PIEZO2 where a mutagenesis approach revealed differential effects on the ability to respond to poking and stretch (Verkest et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation.

claim: The analysis of OSCA1.2 mutants demonstrates the involvement of the AH and residues at the membrane fenestration in the MA response of OSCAs.
source: Overall, the analysis of these mutants demonstrates the involvement of the AH and residues at the membrane fenestration in the MA response of OSCAs, as we initially proposed (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation.

claim: The participation of residues from TM4 and TM6 hint at further similarities with TMEM16 family.
source: The participation of residues from TM4 and TM6 hint at further similarities with TMEM16 family, but to what extent is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation.

claim: The selective disruption of poke-activated currents of OSCA1.2 without affecting its response to membrane stretch suggests that changes in these features could serve to fine-tune the response to certain mechanical stimuli.
source: Perhaps the most surprising result is the selective disruption of poke-activated currents of OSCA1.2 without affecting its response to membrane stretch, which suggests that changes in these features could serve to fine-tune the response to certain mechanical stimuli and may be a source of functional diversity within this large family.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Changes in the AH and lipid-interacting residues may be a source of functional diversity within the OSCA/TMEM63 family.
source: Perhaps the most surprising result is the selective disruption of poke-activated currents of OSCA1.2 without affecting its response to membrane stretch, which suggests that changes in these features could serve to fine-tune the response to certain mechanical stimuli and may be a source of functional diversity within this large family.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the data.
